title: Double treble lace wrap
subtitle: Vertical columns of double treble with ch-1 gaps for a high-drape lace rectangle in lace weight on a 3 mm hook
excerpt: Double treble (UK dtr) produces a tall, open stitch that sets naturally into vertical columns with chain-1 gaps between. Worked in lace-weight yarn on a 3 mm hook, the fabric is light, drapey, and translucent. This rectangle wrap measures 190 cm wide by 55 cm deep and is worked from one short end to the other in a simple column repeat adapted from Therese de Dillmont's Encyclopedia of Needlework.
sourceNotes: Double treble column lace construction adapted from Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), chapter on crochet lace stitches describing tall-stitch open column patterns. Internet Archive: archive.org/details/encyclopaediaofn00dill.
heroPrompt: A lace-weight crochet wrap in ivory or pale grey, draped over a chair in natural light. The vertical column structure and the open ch-1 gaps between double trebles give a translucent lace appearance.

crochet.gaugeText: 1 dtr + ch-1 space = 1.2 cm wide. 2 rows = 2 cm tall. 10 column repeats = 12 cm wide. Gauge in lace weight on a 3 mm hook, measured after blocking.
crochet.finishedSizeText: Approximately 190 cm wide x 55 cm deep, blocked.

glossaryTerms.definition: A tall UK crochet stitch: yarn over three times before inserting the hook, then draw up a loop and work off pairs of loops four times. The same stitch as US triple crochet (trc). Taller than a treble (tr), producing an open, airy column.

A crochet lace structure where tall stitches (treble, double treble, or taller) are worked into the chain spaces of the previous row, maintaining vertical columns of stitches with chain gaps between them. The fabric reads as vertical stripes.

content.text: This lace wrap uses a simple two-row repeat of
double treble
columns separated by single chain spaces. The stitch structure comes from a Victorian needlework encyclopaedia. A
column lace

fabric in lace weight is light on the hook. The stitch count per row stays the same throughout. The two skills to manage are consistent tension on the dtr post and accurate placement into each ch-1 space below.

Lace weight yarn on a 3 mm hook requires careful tension management. The ch-4 turning chain that substitutes for the first dtr must match the height of the dtr columns; if your chain is consistently looser or tighter than your stitch posts, try adjusting to a 3.5 mm hook for the turning chains only. Blocking is not optional for lace weight: it sets the column lines and opens the ch-1 gaps to their full width.

attrs.title: Materials
attrs.body: Approximately 300 g lace-weight yarn (merino-silk or merino-cashmere blends give drape and strength; pure mohair is not recommended as it is difficult to rip back and re-work). A 3 mm hook (US D/3). Tapestry needle. Craft scissors. Blocking mat and rust-proof pins. Tape measure.

content.text: Gauge

1 dtr + 1 ch-1 space = 1.2 cm wide; 2 rows (1 dtr row + 1 return row) = 2 cm tall. Work a swatch of 10 column repeats across for 6 rows, block it fully by soaking, pinning, and drying, then measure the central area. At gauge, 10 repeats should span 12 cm. Lace gauge shifts significantly during blocking; always block the swatch before measuring.
Stitches used
ch: chain -- UK and US shared.
sl st: slip stitch -- UK and US shared.
dc: double crochet (UK) -- used at both edges of each row. The same move as US single crochet (sc).
tr: treble (UK) -- used in the foundation row to set column width. The same move as US double crochet (dc).
dtr: double treble (UK)
-- yarn over 3 times, insert hook, draw up loop, (yarn over, draw through 2 loops) 4 times. The same move as US triple crochet (trc).
Pattern

The wrap is worked from one short end to the other. The long measurement (190 cm) is set by the foundation chain; the depth (55 cm) builds up over rows. The ch-4 turning chain at the start of each dtr row counts as the first dtr.
Foundation chain
Ch 320. (This gives 159 dtr + 158 ch-1 spaces + 2 edge stitches = 319 working positions, plus 1 turning chain.)
Row 1 (right side, foundation row)
Ch 4 (counts as first dtr). *Ch 1. Skip 1 ch. 1 dtr in next ch.* Repeat from * to * across to last ch. 1 dtr in last ch. Turn. (160 dtr including turning ch, 158 ch-1 spaces)
Row 2 (wrong side, return row)
Ch 1 (does not count as a stitch). 1 dc in first dtr. *Ch 1. 1 dc in next ch-1 space.* Repeat from * to * to last dtr. Ch 1. 1 dc in top of turning ch. Turn. (160 dc, 159 ch-1 spaces)
Row 3 (right side, dtr column row)
Ch 4 (counts as first dtr). *1 dtr in next ch-1 space. Ch 1.* Repeat from * to * to last dc. 1 dtr in last dc. Turn. (160 dtr including turning ch, 158 ch-1 spaces)
Rows 4 to 55 -- full repeat
Rows 2 and 3 form the two-row
column lace

repeat. Continue repeating rows 2 and 3 until the work measures 55 cm from the foundation chain. At 2 cm per two-row repeat the depth reaches 55 cm after approximately 55 rows total (including the foundation row). End with a completed return row (row 2 pattern). Fasten off, leaving a 20 cm tail.
Finishing

Weave in all ends using a fine tapestry needle, drawing the tail through the backs of several stitches and reversing direction to secure without a knot. Blocking is essential for lace weight: soak the finished wrap in cool water for 15 minutes, roll gently in a towel, then pin to the stated dimensions on a blocking mat. Pin the long edges first at 5 cm intervals, then pin the short ends. Leave until completely dry before unpinning.
Care

Handwash in cool water with a gentle lace or delicate wash. Do not wring or tumble-dry. Roll in a clean towel, then block flat to restore shape. Store folded away from direct light; lace-weight fibres fade if left in strong sunlight.
What to try next

Replacing the ch-1 gaps with ch-2 opens the column structure further and produces a more open mesh. Working the same column repeat in DK weight on a 4.5 mm hook gives a much faster, denser fabric that reads as textured stripes rather than lace. A ch-3 space between every third column pair produces a grouped-column variation found in Victorian needlework references of the same period.
